summary.text: Nylon is a family of synthetic polymers characterized by amide linkages.
As thermoplastics, nylons can be melt-processed into fibers, films and diverse shapes.
Nylon was the first commercially successful synthetic thermoplastic polymer, and Wallace Hume Carothers made the first one at DuPont.

paragraphs.heading: What nylon is
paragraphs.text: Nylon is a family of synthetic polymers whose units are joined by amide linkages. Nylons are thermoplastics, so they can be melted and shaped into fibres, films and many other forms. One family, called nylon-XY, is made from diamines and dicarboxylic acids with carbon chains of length X and Y, and nylon-6,6 is an important member. Another family, nylon-Z, comes from aminocarboxylic acids with chain length Z.

paragraphs.heading: Where it is used
paragraphs.text: Nylon turns up in textiles and fibres such as clothing, flooring and rubber reinforcement, in moulded parts for cars and electrical equipment, and in films, mostly for wrapping food. Its properties are often adjusted by blending in additives. Nylons are generally brownish and can feel soft, and some varieties look like silk.

paragraphs.heading: A research bet at DuPont
paragraphs.text: Nylon came out of DuPont, whose earlier work on rayon, a fibre based on cellulose, paved the way for it. In 1927 Charles Stine proposed splitting the chemical department into small teams doing pioneering research that would lead to practical uses. Wallace Hume Carothers, an instructor at Harvard, was hired to run the polymer group, and at first he was free to do pure research testing Hermann Staudinger's theories. The whole effort lasted eleven years, from 1927 to nylon's announcement in 1938.

paragraphs.heading: From paste to fibre
paragraphs.text: By spring 1930 Carothers's team had made two new polymers: neoprene, a synthetic rubber later widely used in World War II, and an elastic paste that grew very strong as it cooled, the future nylon. The team was then steered away from pure research toward finding one chemical combination suited to industry. A coworker, Julian W. Hill, had made a polyester by cold drawing in 1930, and Carothers later used that method to develop nylon. On February 28, 1935, Carothers made the first nylon, nylon 66, at the DuPont Experimental Station. It had the elasticity and strength the team wanted, but needed a complex manufacturing process.

paragraphs.heading: Toothbrushes and stockings
paragraphs.text: DuPont patented the polymer in September 1938 and quickly held a monopoly on the fibre. Carothers had died 16 months before the announcement, so he never saw his success. The name came from reworking norun, meaning no run, into a unique word that was never trademarked. The first commercial use was a toothbrush with nylon bristles in 1938; women's stockings followed. They were displayed at the 1939 New York World's Fair, went on sale in 1940, and sold 64 million pairs in their first year.

paragraphs.heading: War and industry
paragraphs.text: During World War II almost all nylon went to the military for parachutes and parachute cord, and wartime uses grew the market for nylon and other plastics. Making nylon took three DuPont departments working together: Chemical Research, Ammonia and Rayon. Some key ingredients needed high-pressure chemistry, the Ammonia Department's specialty, and nylon's reactants soon made up half that department's sales, helping it through the Great Depression. The first nylon plant, at Seaford, Delaware, began commercial production on December 15, 1939.
